articles.description:
I recently watched Matt Pocock's workshop, Full Walkthrough: Workflow for AI Coding.
The main takeaway: Good AI-assisted coding is not about writing better prompts. It's about applying solid software engineering practices to AI agents.
Here are the key lessons.
LLMs tend to become less reliable as their context grows.
Matt describes two zones:
Smart Zone: Fresh context, focused tasks, better decisions.
Dumb Zone: Bloated context, reduced reliability, more mistakes.
He uses roughly 100K tokens as a practical warning threshold, not a universal technical limit.
His recommendations:
Break large tasks into smaller, independent tasks.
Keep system instructions minimal.
Prefer clearing context and restarting with well-defined tasks rather than repeatedly compacting long conversations.

articles.author: jian xu
articles.description:
Spend your time on the work, not the terminal.
I'm the developer of xtty, a native macOS terminal for everyday shell, SSH and coding-agent work. The goal is to reduce repeated setup and switching between sessions, so you can stay focused on the work you opened the terminal to do.
Connect to servers: open several saved SSH hosts together, including configured jump-host routes.
Handle repeated password prompts: use configured matching rules and saved credentials for automatic filling.
Open another remote shell: Duplicate Tab starts a fresh, independent SSH connection to the same server and restores the remote working directory.
Move files: transfer files with sz/rz using native macOS file dialogs.
Work across sessions: arrange tabs and split panes, broadcast input to selected panes, and see coding-agent status indicators.
These features share one purpose: spend less time recreating the working environment and more time using it.
The walkthrough shows the real app with fictional servers and terminal data:
  
  



  
  
  A concrete example: opening a second SSH shell


Suppose a command is running on a server and you want a separate shell in the same project directory. Duplicate Tab opens another connection and restores that directory, while the original shell stays separate.
It does not clone running processes or preserve a session across disconnections. For persistent remote sessions, tools such as tmux address a different need. With broadcast input, check the selected destinations before entering commands.
xtty is proprietary and macOS-only, with Apple Silicon and Intel downloads. There is a Free edition, a seven-day Pro trial, and an optional US$29.90 one-time Pro purchase. No subscription.
iTerm2 remains a mature, free, open-source choice. xtty focuses on making everyday connection, session and file-transfer workflows accessible directly in the UI.
Website and downloads
Which repeated step in your terminal workflow would you most like to remove?
articles.title: xtty — A terminal that makes everyday work easier

articles.author: Ujjwal Dubey
articles.description:
Owners often ask why a search engine or an AI assistant describes their business strangely, or not at all. One common, boring cause: the words on the homepage only exist after JavaScript runs. Some crawlers render pages fully. Others read the raw HTML and move on. If your headline, your services and your city are not in that raw HTML, part of the web may never see them.
Here is a quick way to compare what a person sees with what a simple crawler sees, in about thirty lines of Python.
import re, html, requests

def visible_text(markup: str) -> str:
    markup = re.sub(r"<(script|style|noscript)[^>]*>.*?</\1>", " ", markup, flags=re.S | re.I)
    text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", markup)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(text)).strip()

url = "https://www.example.com/"
raw = requests…
articles.title: Raw HTML vs Rendered: A Quick Check of What Crawlers Actually Read on Your Homepage

articles.description:
A developer captured a Claude Code API request that was 594,750 bytes. After GZIP compression, the body was 289,145 bytes. That's about 51% less data to upload, without removing a word from the request.
Those numbers come from a community investigation, not an official Anthropic benchmark. But they help explain a small change that shipped on October 14, 2026: Claude Code v2.1.300 began compressing large requests to api.anthropic.com with GZIP, including when telemetry is disabled.
GZIP has been around since 1992. Brotli is newer and often produces smaller compressed files. So why pick GZIP for an AI coding tool in 2026? And what should we use in our own APIs?
A coding assistant's request can include conversation history, tool definitions, tool results, and other context. What gets included…
articles.title: Claude Code Added GZIP in 2026. Why Not Brotli?
